questions.title: How does § 1252 give the Tenth Circuit jurisdiction here, and what exactly is encompassed by “final orders of removal” for consolidated review?
questions.question_body: The panel says it exercises jurisdiction under 8 U.S.C. § 1252 and cites § 1252(a)(1) and (b)(9) for consolidated review of asylum claims. I'm confused about the scope of § 1252(b)(9). Why is this petition characterized as a review of a “final order of removal,” and how does that allow the court to consider the asylum denial alongside it? Also, are there any jurisdictional limits (like the criminal alien bar or exhaustion requirements) that the court implicitly found satisfied, and how does that analysis typically get done when it isn’t spelled out?

questions.title: Why doesn’t the court discuss Article III standing in petitions for review of removal orders?
questions.question_body: There’s no standing section. Is it because being subject to a final order of removal obviously constitutes an injury-in-fact traceable to the agency and redressable by a court order? In immigration petitions for review, is standing analysis usually omitted as a matter of course, and if so, what are the doctrinal reasons for that practice?

questions.title: Why does the court treat “past persecution” as a factual question reviewed for substantial evidence rather than a mixed question of law and fact?
questions.question_body: The opinion states that whether a noncitizen proved past private persecution is a fact question reviewed under the substantial-evidence standard. But 'persecution' is a legally defined concept (albeit undefined in the statute and fleshed out by case law). Why is the Tenth Circuit reviewing this as a factual finding rather than applying de novo review to at least the legal component? How does this fit with other circuits that characterize persecution or 'nexus' as mixed questions?

questions.title: How does the substantial-evidence standard work when the record supports multiple plausible inferences?
questions.question_body: The panel repeatedly says there is 'substantial evidence' for the BIA’s findings. I struggle with how to evaluate this: if the record would allow both the petitioners’ inference (political motive) and the agency’s inference (retaliation for a property dispute), is the court’s role simply to ask whether a reasonable adjudicator could choose the agency’s view, even if the court might pick the other? What does it mean for evidence to be so strong that 'any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled' to reach the opposite conclusion?

questions.title: Why are threats and psychological harm deemed insufficient to constitute persecution in the Tenth Circuit?
questions.question_body: The court says 'threats alone are insufficient,' and it downplays psychological harms like insomnia and panic attacks. Some circuits have recognized death threats as persecution in certain contexts. What is the Tenth Circuit’s doctrinal basis for requiring more than threats and psychological harm, and are there circumstances in this circuit where threats alone can qualify (e.g., especially menacing death threats, accompanied by specific targeting or evidence of capability)?

questions.title: How did the court analyze the 'nexus' requirement and decide political opinion was only tangential?
questions.question_body: The opinion emphasizes that the escalated threats began after Jimenez intervened in a property dispute with 'Don Rafa,' and it treats that non-political conflict as the central motive. But petitioners had earlier received threats referencing the Liberal Party and campaigning. Why did the court discount those earlier threats as establishing or corroborating a political motive? What principles govern how the agency and court weigh temporally separated incidents and infer the primary motive in mixed-motive cases under the 'one central reason' standard?

questions.title: What is the legal source for the 'government unable or unwilling to control' requirement when the persecutor is a private actor?
questions.question_body: The definition of 'refugee' in § 1101(a)(42)(A) doesn’t expressly mention private actors, yet the court applies the familiar unable-or-unwilling test. What precedents or interpretive principles in the Tenth Circuit ground importing this requirement into the statutory text, and how does the court justify it as a matter of statutory interpretation?

questions.title: Why did the court rely on a Seventh Circuit articulation of 'systemic' government failure, and is that standard binding in the Tenth Circuit?
questions.question_body: The opinion cites Osorio-Morales (7th Cir.) for the idea that evidence of 'systemic, rather than individual, failures' is often required to show a government is unwilling or unable to protect. Does the Tenth Circuit endorse that 'systemic' framing as its own rule, or is it using it persuasively? How does this square with Tenth Circuit cases that seem to accept evidence of localized police inaction when combined with futility/danger in reporting?

questions.title: How much reporting to authorities is required before concluding a government is unwilling or unable to protect?
questions.question_body: The court faults petitioners for 'minimal' outreach and emphasizes they didn’t pursue channels beyond conversations with two officers, even though one officer suggested police were contributing to the problem. Why did the court view that as insufficient to establish futility or danger in reporting? What kinds of evidence typically satisfy the futility/danger exception in the Tenth Circuit, especially when there is some evidence of law-enforcement corruption or alignment with persecutors?

questions.title: Why did the court discuss internal relocation burdens using the government’s rebuttal standard when no presumption applied?
questions.question_body: The opinion quotes the regulation about the government rebutting the presumption of future persecution via internal relocation, but it also says petitioners never established past persecution (so no presumption). In that posture, isn’t the burden on the applicant to show that relocation isn’t reasonable under § 1208.13(b)(2)–(3)? Is the court offering an alternative holding ('even if they had a presumption, the government could rebut via relocation')? How should we read the burden-shifting discussion here?

questions.title: How probative is the continued safety of family members in assessing internal relocation?
questions.question_body: The court leans on the fact that petitioners’ relatives remain unharmed in Colombia and that petitioners briefly lived safely with Jimenez’s mother. Petitioners argued family presence doesn’t always establish safety. Why did the court view family safety as strong evidence favoring reasonable relocation in this case? Are there Tenth Circuit or BIA principles that limit how much weight adjudicators should assign to family safety, especially where persecutors allegedly have national reach?

questions.title: Under what circumstances may the court 'consult the IJ’s more complete explanation' when reviewing a single-member BIA affirmance?
questions.question_body: The panel cites Uanreroro to say it primarily reviews the BIA decision but can consult the IJ’s fuller reasoning. What are the boundaries of that practice? If the BIA’s reasoning is thin or ambiguous, can the court rely on IJ rationales the BIA didn’t expressly adopt without running afoul of the Chenery principle (no post hoc rationalizations)?

questions.title: Why does the court limit review to the administrative record and not consider developments after removal proceedings?
questions.question_body: The court says it’s limited to the administrative record under § 1252(b)(4)(A). If new evidence arose (e.g., fresh threats), why can’t the court consider it on petition for review? Is the appropriate avenue a motion to reopen before the BIA, and how does that procedural posture interact with pending petitions for review?

questions.title: How does the court treat unbriefed theories (like the 'particular social group' of 'social leaders')—waiver, forfeiture, or failure to exhaust?
questions.question_body: The panel says petitioners didn’t brief PSG arguments and limits review to political opinion. Is that characterized as waiver in the court of appeals or failure to exhaust at the agency? What’s the doctrinal consequence—outright abandonment on appeal, or could the court remand if the BIA had addressed PSG but petitioners failed to brief it here?

questions.title: What weight do unpublished Tenth Circuit decisions carry in asylum reviews, and why did the court cite several?
questions.question_body: The opinion cites unpublished Tenth Circuit cases (e.g., Chhetri, Carias-Mejia). Are these cited purely for persuasive value under Tenth Circuit Rule 32.1, and how does the court decide when unpublished cases sufficiently state or apply circuit law, especially on recurring issues like threats-as-persecution or the asylum/withholding standard interplay?

questions.title: Why didn’t the court address the due process right-to-counsel claim the BIA rejected?
questions.question_body: The panel notes petitioners did not appeal the due process claim. Is that treated as waiver/abandonment because it wasn’t raised in the opening brief? If so, would the court have had an independent obligation to consider structural due process errors, or is it entirely forfeitable? Also, how does the prejudice standard for right-to-counsel claims interact with the substantial-evidence framework if it had been reviewed?

questions.title: How did the court apply the 'one central reason' standard to dismiss a mixed-motive political opinion claim?
questions.question_body: The court recognizes persecutors can have multiple motives but says political opinion must be more than 'incidental, tangential, superficial, or subordinate.' What analytical steps does the Tenth Circuit use to distinguish central from tangential motives? Here, the record included explicit references to 'snitches from [the] Liberal Party'—why were those not enough to show political opinion was at least one central reason?

questions.title: Why does failure on asylum necessarily doom withholding of removal in this case?
questions.question_body: The court says petitioners fail asylum and thus necessarily fail withholding because withholding has a higher standard. Is that always true, or could differing burdens (no discretion, different nexus standard under § 1231(b)(3)) ever allow a petitioner to lose asylum but win withholding? What specific elements here foreclosed withholding once asylum failed?
